newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour's Blair on defensive in Scotland.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour's Blair on defensive in Scotland.

text.p: Britain's opposition leader Tony Blair was forced on to the defensive on Friday for the first time in the election campaign when the launch of Labour's Scottish manifesto was overshadowed by criticism of his party's devolution plans.
Blair, born and educated in Edinburgh, ran into a barrage of hostile questioning over the tax-raising powers of Labour's planned Scottish parliament that left him clearly exasperated.
"Is there anyone who would like to ask a question about anything else?" Blair asked after 30 minutes of grilling at a press conference.
Blair, leader since 1994, has never held a ministerial post and his opponents have targeted his lack of inexperience, particularly "under fire".
Blair did not lose his temper but the frustration was clearly evident that he was unable to talk about his preferred issues of health and education.
One of the few differences between Labour, out of power since 1979, and the ruling Conservatives is Labour's plans for widespread constitutional change.

If it wins the May 1 election, Labour intends to hold a referendum by the autumn in Scotland to establish a parliament in Edinburgh that would have the power to vary income tax by as much as three percentage points for Scottish taxpayers.
The Labour Party, however, has firmly ruled out any increase in income tax for the next five years. Blair was bombarded with critical questions about the apparent paradox.

What was the point of granting powers if he would not let them be exercised? Would parliament in London have a veto over a Scottish parliament's tax decisions? Could Blair conceive of circumstances in which the revenue-varying power would ever be used?
Blair fielded all the questions by repeating his mantra that, while he could not speak for other parties in Scotland, Labour -- the dominant party in Scotland -- had no plans to raise taxes.
"The Scottish Labour Party has no proposals to raise taxes. That commitment applies here in Scotland just as it applies in England," he said. "Having a power is not the same as using a power."

The manifesto launch had already been soured by an interview Blair gave to the Scotsman newspaper on Friday in which he likened the Edinburgh parliament's proposed tax powers to those of a parish council.
Blair defended his comments, saying that constitutionally parliament in London would be devolving powers but not ceding sovereignty if it legislated to create a Scottish parliament.

This, he said, was a sensible third way between the ruling Conservative Party's refusal to countenance any alteration to the Union of the countries that make up Britain and what he called the Scottish Nationalist Party's "lunatic" plans for independence.
The Labour manifesto was a Scottish version of the national one released in London on Thursday.

The back cover is covered with a tartan of the Blair clan made up of a blue and green pattern with a thin thread of red running through it -- a fitting metaphor for what remains of full-blooded socialism in Blair's New Labour.
